title: Build & Deploy a Website
subtitle: From zero to a live site the world can visit
description: Build a real personal website from scratch with HTML & CSS, then deploy it to GitHub Pages so anyone on the internet can see it.
learningOutcomes: Understand how websites work (HTML structure, CSS styling, browser rendering)
Write real HTML with headings, paragraphs, links, images, and navigation
Style a site with CSS — colors, fonts, spacing, and responsive layout
Use Git to track changes and push code to GitHub
Deploy a live website to GitHub Pages with a public URL
Share a real link that anyone in the world can open

artifact.initialState: no files, no site, nothing exists yet
artifact.finalState: a live personal website deployed on GitHub Pages with a public URL
artifact.previewIfNoProgress: No website yet — let's build one

goals.title: Plan your site
goals.goal: Decide what your website is about and what content goes on it — even a rough sketch is enough.
goals.outcome: You know what your site is called, what it's about, and roughly what goes on the page.
goals.coachAsk: Help me plan a personal website. I'm not sure where to start — what should I think about before writing any code?
goals.doneWhen: The learner can describe in one sentence what their site is about and roughly what will be on it.
tips: A personal site only needs one page to start
Think: who is this for? what do they need to see?
Keep it simple — you can always add more later

concepts: what a website actually is (files a browser reads)
the difference between HTML (structure) and CSS (style)
pages, navigation, and content hierarchy
commonMistakes: trying to plan every pixel before writing any code
making it too complicated — multiple pages, forms, databases
not choosing a topic and getting stuck in analysis paralysis
successExamples: I want a simple page about my cat with a photo, a bio, and a contact email
I want a portfolio with my name, what I do, and three project cards
teachingContext.whyItMatters: A clear plan means every line of code has a purpose — no wasted effort.

goals.title: Create your first HTML file
goals.goal: Set up a project folder and write a valid HTML file that opens in a browser.
goals.outcome: A file called index.html that opens in your browser and shows some text.
goals.coachAsk: Help me create my first HTML file. I have a plan for my site — now I need to set up a folder and write the code. Open Terminal or Finder and walk me through it.
goals.doneWhen: A file named index.html exists in a project folder and opens in a browser showing visible content.
tips: index.html is the standard name for a homepage
You can open any .html file by double-clicking it
Don't worry about making it pretty yet — just get text on screen

concepts: HTML document skeleton (doctype, html, head, body)
what goes in <head> (title, charset, viewport) vs <body> (visible content)
opening the file in a browser to preview
commonMistakes: forgetting the closing </body> or </html> tags
putting visible content inside <head> instead of <body>
naming the file something other than index.html and getting confused later
successExamples: Double-click index.html and you see your text in the browser
The browser tab shows your page title
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Every website starts with a single HTML file — this is the foundation everything else builds on.

goals.title: Add real content
goals.goal: Fill the page with actual content — a heading, paragraphs, a link, and an image.
goals.outcome: The page has a title, some text about you or your topic, a clickable link, and an image.
goals.coachAsk: My HTML file exists but it's mostly empty. Help me add real content — a heading, some paragraphs, maybe a link and an image.
goals.doneWhen: The page has at least a heading, a paragraph, one link, and one image (or clear placeholder).
tips: Use <h1> for the main title, <h2> for section headings
Images need both a file and alt text:
Links use text

concepts: heading hierarchy (h1 through h6 — don't skip levels)
paragraphs with
anchor links with <a href>
images with and alt text
what alt text is for (accessibility + broken image fallback)
commonMistakes: using headings just to make text big (use CSS for that)
forgetting alt text on images
putting block content inside inline elements (e.g. a heading inside a link)
using absolute URLs for local images that won't work when deployed
successExamples: The page clearly tells a story: title → intro → details → link
Images load and have descriptive alt text
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Content is why people visit your site. Without real content, it's just an empty frame.

goals.title: Style with CSS
goals.goal: Make the page look intentional with colors, fonts, spacing, and layout.
goals.outcome: The page has a background color, readable fonts, proper spacing, and looks designed rather than raw.
goals.coachAsk: My page has content but it looks like a plain document. Help me add CSS to make it look like a real website — colors, fonts, and layout.
goals.doneWhen: The page has custom colors, fonts, spacing, and at least one layout technique (centering, flexbox, or grid).
tips: A <style> tag in <head> is the fastest way to start
body { font-family: system-ui; } gives you a modern font for free
margin: 0 auto; centers content; max-width keeps it readable

concepts: CSS selectors (element, class, id)
the box model (margin, border, padding, content)
flexbox for layout (display: flex, justify-content, align-items)
responsive units (rem, %, max-width) vs fixed pixels
color: hex vs named colors vs rgb
commonMistakes: using !important to fix specificity issues instead of learning selectors
hardcoding pixel widths that break on different screens
putting CSS inline (style="...") instead of in a stylesheet or <style> block
not testing at different browser widths
successExamples: The page looks clean and intentional at desktop width
Content is centered and has breathing room
Fonts are readable and consistent
teachingContext.whyItMatters: CSS is the difference between a document and a designed experience. It's what makes people stay.

goals.title: Make it responsive
goals.goal: Ensure the site looks good on phones, tablets, and desktops.
goals.outcome: The site adapts to different screen sizes — text is readable, nothing overflows, images scale.
goals.coachAsk: My site looks good on my laptop but probably breaks on a phone. Help me make it responsive so it works everywhere.
goals.doneWhen: The site looks usable at 320px width (phone) and 1200px+ (desktop) with no horizontal scrolling.
tips: The viewport meta tag is required: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
max-width: 100% on images prevents overflow
Media queries (@media) change styles at different breakpoints

concepts: the viewport meta tag (without it, phones render at 960px)
mobile-first design (style for small screens first, add complexity for large)
media queries (@media screen and (min-width: 768px))
flexible units (%, vw, rem) vs fixed pixels
flex-wrap for multi-item layouts
commonMistakes: forgetting the viewport meta tag entirely
using fixed pixel widths on containers
designing for desktop first and bolting on mobile later
not testing on an actual phone or narrow browser window
successExamples: Open the site on your phone and it looks like it was made for it
Resize the browser window and content reflows smoothly
No horizontal scrollbar at any width
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Over half of web traffic is mobile. A site that only works on desktop is broken for most people.

goals.title: Add more pages
goals.goal: Create a second page and link between pages with a consistent navigation menu.
goals.outcome: At least two pages exist (e.g. index.html + about.html) with a nav that links between them.
goals.coachAsk: My one page looks great. Help me add a second page — like an About or Projects page — and link them together so visitors can navigate.
goals.doneWhen: A second .html file exists with real content, and a <nav> element on both pages links between them.
tips: Copy index.html as a starting point for the new page
Keep the nav identical on both pages (same links, same order)
Use relative links: <a href="about.html"> not absolute paths

concepts: relative vs absolute paths
consistent navigation across pages
the <nav> semantic element
copy-paste as a starting point (DRY comes later)
commonMistakes: using different nav structures on different pages
broken links because of wrong file paths
putting the nav inside the wrong element
copying the page but forgetting to update the <title>
successExamples: Clicking About in the nav takes you to about.html and back
Both pages share the same visual style and nav layout
The browser tab title is different on each page
teachingContext.whyItMatters: A website with one page is a flyer. Multiple pages with navigation is a site.

goals.title: Push to GitHub
goals.goal: Initialize a Git repo and push your site to GitHub so it's backed up and ready to deploy.
goals.outcome: Your site code is on GitHub in a repository with all your files committed.
goals.coachAsk: My site is done locally. Help me put it on GitHub so it's saved online and ready to deploy.
goals.doneWhen: A GitHub repository exists with all site files committed and pushed.
tips: git init → git add . → git commit → git push
Add a .gitignore with just .DS_Store to keep macOS junk out
Name the repo something simple like my-website

concepts: Git tracks changes to files over time
git init, git add, git commit, git push — the core loop
GitHub is where your Git repo lives online
README.md is the file GitHub shows on the repo homepage
commonMistakes: running git commands in the wrong directory
committing before adding files (git add first)
forgetting to create the GitHub repo before pushing
pushing to main vs main branch naming confusion
successExamples: git status shows 'nothing to commit' and git remote -v shows your GitHub URL
Opening github.com/YOU/repo-name shows all your files
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Git is your safety net — you can always go back. GitHub is where your code lives before it goes live.

goals.title: Deploy to GitHub Pages
goals.goal: Turn your GitHub repo into a live website with a public URL anyone can visit.
goals.outcome: Your site is live at https://yourusername.github.io/repo-name/ and you can share the link.
goals.coachAsk: My code is on GitHub. Help me deploy it to GitHub Pages so I can share a live link with anyone.
goals.doneWhen: A browser is visible showing the site loaded at a public https://username.github.io/... URL — not a local file:// path — with the site content visible and no 404 error.
tips: Settings → Pages → Source: main branch → Save
It takes 1-2 minutes to deploy the first time
If it 404s, check that your main file is named index.html

concepts: GitHub Pages serves your repo as a website for free
Settings → Pages → choose your branch
the deployment URL format: username.github.io/repo-name
pushing a new commit triggers automatic redeployment
commonMistakes: forgetting to enable GitHub Pages in Settings
selecting the wrong branch (use main, not a feature branch)
naming the file something other than index.html (GitHub Pages looks for index.html as the homepage)
not waiting long enough for the first deploy
successExamples: The URL loads and shows your site exactly as it looks locally
You can share the link and someone else can open it
Pushing a change to GitHub updates the live site within minutes
teachingContext.whyItMatters: This is the moment your work becomes real — a URL you can put in your bio, share with friends, or add to a resume.

goals.title: Share your site
goals.goal: Open your live site, verify everything works, and share the link.
goals.outcome: You've opened your live site in a browser, confirmed it looks right, and have the URL ready to share.
goals.coachAsk: My site is deployed! Help me open it, check that everything looks right, and grab the link so I can share it.
goals.doneWhen: A browser window is visible showing the deployed site at a public GitHub Pages URL (https://username.github.io/...) — not a local file:// path — with the correct content and styling visible.
tips: Open in a private/incognito window to see the fresh version
Test every link and page
Copy the URL — you earned it

concepts: cache busting (hard refresh or incognito for fresh deploys)
testing navigation across pages on the live version
what to share: the URL in a bio, message, or social post
commonMistakes: checking the cached old version and thinking deploy failed
forgetting to test links on the live site (not just locally)
not saving the URL
successExamples: The live site loads with correct content, styling, and navigation
All links work on the live version
You have the URL copied and ready to share
teachingContext.whyItMatters: Building something is great. Sharing it is what makes it matter.
